paras: The Safford ballot box incident was an episode in Dallas County, Alabama, on the afternoon of the state election of August 4, 1890, in which a few armed men from Selma, sent out on the sheriff's orders, dispersed a crowd of Black people at the Safford polling place and carried off the ballot box. No one was reported hurt, and the only account, a Selma dispatch, claimed the crowd had planned to seize the box. Newspapers across the country carried the dispatch inside reports of a Democratic sweep and light Black turnout, and a Kansas paper reprinted it to dispute it.

The episode was reported in a Birmingham wire story of August 5 on the Alabama state election, which said returns showed a large Democratic victory. The same dispatch said that in Jefferson County few Black men came to the polls, "stating that they did not care to vote."

According to a special to the Birmingham Age-Herald from Selma, there was "danger of serious trouble in Dallas" at one point on election afternoon. The correspondent wrote that "the negroes had planned to capture the ballot box at Safford when the polls closed." In response, a few armed men from Selma went out under orders from the sheriff, "dispersed the mob and brought in the box." The dispatch closed by saying that the Black crowd "dispersed quietly."
No report of arrests, injuries or any inquiry appears in the coverage, and neither the sheriff nor any member of the armed party is named.

The Selma paragraph traveled with the Birmingham election wire and appeared on August 5 and 6 in papers from Washington and Alexandria to New York, Richmond, Savannah, Fort Worth, Omaha, Salt Lake City, Helena and Salem. Weeklies kept printing it into mid-August, with the Butler Weekly Times in Missouri adding "it is alleged" and the Manning Times in South Carolina running it on August 20. Headlines framed the story around Black non-voting and Democratic success: "A White Man's Victory" in Omaha, "There Was No Use in Voting" in Salem, and "Few Negroes Voted. But They Planned a Raid on the Ballet Box" in Helena.

The Washington Evening Star went further than the text it headed, titling the story "Negroes Try to Capture a Ballot Box, but Armed Whites Prevent It." The Savannah Morning News, by contrast, placed the same paragraph under "No Serious Trouble Reported From Any Part of the State." The New-York Tribune said the armed men "scattered the mob," while the Portland Daily Press condensed the story into a brief saying a "riot" had been feared on Monday.

The Leavenworth Advocate in Kansas reprinted the dispatch on August 16 under "Negroes Not Voting" and answered it in an editorial. Its editor called the dispatch "self-contradictory," since it said Black men had stayed away from the polls and also that they tried to take the ballot box. Accepting only the first claim, the paper said a Black man who did not vote did so "simply because his life was in danger there as elsewhere in the South," and it urged passage of the Federal Election Bill then before Congress.

The only account of a planned seizure of the ballot box comes from the Selma correspondent, whose dispatch also reported that the armed men acted under the sheriff's orders. The Leavenworth Advocate rejected that account on its internal logic rather than on any separate report from Safford. The place name also varies in print, appearing as "Safford" in most copies, "Suffard" in the Advocate and "Safforl" in the Portland Daily Press.

reader.title: Safford ballot box incident
bases: Armed white men sent out by the sheriff dispersed a Black crowd at a polling place on election day and took the ballot box; no one is reported hurt (A1, A15).

Every copy traces to one Age-Herald special from Selma (A1); the only other voice, a Leavenworth editorial, reprints that dispatch and doubts its account of a seizure plan without independent knowledge of the place (A15).

accounts.label: Age-Herald special from Selma (wire)
accounts.gist: There was danger of serious trouble in Dallas on election afternoon; Black people had planned to seize the Safford ballot box at the close of the polls, and armed men from Selma under the sheriff's orders dispersed 'the mob' and brought the box in, after which 'the negroes dispersed quietly.'

accounts.label: Leavenworth Advocate editorial
accounts.gist: The dispatch contradicted itself by saying Black men did not vote and also tried to take the ballot box; the editor believed the first claim and said they stayed away because their lives were in danger.

framing.detail: The Washington Evening Star ran the wire under 'Negroes Try to Capture a Ballot Box, but Armed Whites Prevent It,' turning the dispatch's 'had planned to' into an attempt.

Most papers printed the paragraph inside election-returns stories with headlines about the Democratic sweep and Black non-voting, such as 'A White Man's Victory' (Omaha) and 'There Was No Use in Voting' (Salem).
The Leavenworth Advocate, under 'Negroes Not Voting,' reprinted the dispatch to rebut it, saying Black men stayed from the polls in fear for their lives and calling for the Federal Election Bill.

versions.value: Black people had planned to capture the ballot box and were dispersed by armed men (Selma special)
The seizure story is doubtful; Black men did not vote because their lives were in danger (Leavenworth Advocate editorial)

conflicts.note: The Advocate gives no separate account of events at Safford; it disputes the wire's plausibility from its internal contradiction, not from a local source.

versions.value: Headline: 'Negroes Try to Capture a Ballot Box' (an attempt)
Body text: 'had planned to capture the ballot box' (a plan)

conflicts.note: The Evening Star's headline goes further than the dispatch it heads; no copy describes an actual attempt on the box.

record_check.dossier: Safford: every opened copy of the wire prints 'Safford' (one 'Suffard', one 'Safforl'); none prints 'Stafford'

record_check.record: a crowd of Negroes tried to seize a ballot box
record_check.dossier: The dispatch says only that they 'had planned to' capture the box; no attempt is described, and the claim comes from a Selma special alone and was disputed editorially
'A few armed men from Selma, under orders from the sheriff'
An armed party (a posse) acting on the sheriff's orders; the papers do not call them deputies or say the sheriff was present
At least 16 white papers carried the dispatch, August 5-20, 1890; no Black-press coverage was found
